sources.title: American College of Sports Medicine Position Stand. Resistance Training Prescription for Muscle Function, Hypertrophy, and Physical Performance in Healthy Adults: An Overview of Reviews
sources.authors: Currier BS, D'Souza AC, Singh MAF, Lowisz CV, Rawson ES, Schoenfeld BJ, Smith-Ryan AE, et al.
sources.population_design_dose: Overview of 137 systematic reviews of randomized trials in healthy adults (>=18 y), resistance training >=6 wk; most evidence from novice trainees.
sources.findings: Resistance training improves strength and hypertrophy versus control; strength enhanced by heavier loads, 2-3 sets, >=2 sessions/wk and exercise at session start; hypertrophy by >=10 sets/muscle/wk; training to failure and periodization not consistently influential; perceived-exertion scales can raise absolute load with strength gains; individualization encouraged for adherence.
sources.locator: Abstract; Results (strength, hypertrophy); Discussion subsections Progressive overload, Specificity/Individualization, Variation.
limitations: Overview of reviews dominated by novice trainees; not concurrent-training or runner specific.
No per-session increment, establishment or return procedure is specified.
counterevidence: States progression is not always necessary for benefit, so planned progression is a choice, not a requirement.

sources.title: Individualized Endurance Training Based on Recovery and Training Status in Recreational Runners
sources.authors: Nuuttila OP, Nummela A, Korhonen E, Hakkinen K, Kyrolainen H
sources.population_design_dose: 30 recreational runners, matched-pair randomized, 15 wk; predefined program (2 progressive weeks with +10% volume then a -25% recovery week) versus load adjusted twice weekly from HRV, perceived recovery and HR-speed index.
sources.findings: Both groups improved; individualized group improved 10-km time more (-6.2% versus -2.9%) with fewer low responders; HIT block used 6x3 min at maximal sustainable effort.
limitations: Small sample; HRV-dependent monitoring; negligible strength training.
counterevidence: Predefined progression was also effective.

sources.title: Resistance Exercise Minimal Dose Strategies for Increasing Muscle Strength in the General Population: an Overview
sources.authors: Nuzzo JL, Pinto MD, Kirk BJC, Nosaka K
sources.population_design_dose: Narrative overview of minimal-dose strategies in people not currently resistance training.
sources.findings: Once-weekly sessions and single-set programs (>=4 exercises, >=2 sessions/wk) improve strength versus no exercise.
sources.locator: Abstract; sections on Weekend Warrior and single-set training.
limitations: Overview, not systematic; untrained populations.
counterevidence: Gains concern strength increase in untrained people, not maintenance in hybrid athletes.

sources.title: No effect of a graded training program on the number of running-related injuries in novice runners: a randomized controlled trial
sources.authors: Buist I, Bredeweg SW, van Mechelen W, Lemmink KA, Pepping GJ, Diercks RL
sources.population_design_dose: 532 novice runners; standard 8-week versus graded 13-week (10% rule) program toward a 6.7-km event.
sources.findings: Injury incidence 20.8% graded versus 20.3% standard; no preventive effect of the graded program.
limitations: Abstract only; single event distance.
counterevidence: Does not show that faster progression is safe for every athlete.

sources.title: Excessive progression in weekly running distance and risk of running-related injuries: an association which varies according to type of injury
sources.authors: Nielsen RO, Parner ET, Nohr EA, Sorensen H, Lind M, Rasmussen S
sources.population_design_dose: 874 novice runners with GPS watches, 1 year.
sources.findings: No overall difference in injury rate across <10%, 10-30% and >30% weekly progression; >30% associated with more distance-related injuries (HR 1.59, 95% CI 0.96-2.66).
limitations: Abstract only; exploratory.
counterevidence: Overall injury rates did not differ.

sources.title: The talk test as a useful tool to monitor aerobic exercise intensity in healthy population
sources.authors: Kwon Y, Kang KW, Chang JS
sources.population_design_dose: 17 healthy adults, treadmill cardiopulmonary testing with three talk-test stages.
sources.findings: Talk-test stages correlated strongly with ventilatory and heart-rate markers and rose linearly with intensity.
limitations: Small sample; validation study; not a training outcome.
counterevidence: Effort cues remain approximate; individual thresholds are not measured.

sources.title: Effects of Different Training Intensity Distribution in Recreational Runners
sources.authors: Festa L, Tarperi C, Skroce K, La Torre A, Schena F
sources.population_design_dose: 38 recreational runners, 8 wk, TRIMP-matched polarized (77/3/20) versus focused (40/50/10) distributions.
sources.findings: Both improved velocity at VT, RCP and VO2max, 2-km performance and economy similarly; focused training used 17% less time.
limitations: Heart-rate zones from laboratory testing; 8 weeks.
counterevidence: Does not test effort-only prescriptions.

sources.title: How much running is too much? Identifying high-risk running sessions in a 5200-person cohort study
sources.authors: Schuster Brandt Frandsen J, Hulme A, Parner ET, Moller M, Lindman I, Abrahamson J, et al., Nielsen RO
sources.population_design_dose: 5205 adult runners (mean 45.8 y, 22% female), Garmin GPS data, 588,071 sessions, 18-month follow-up; exposure = single-session distance relative to the longest run in the previous 30 days.
sources.findings: Single-session spikes >10-30%, >30-100% and >100% above the 30-day longest run were associated with higher overuse-injury rates (HRR 1.64, 1.52, 2.28); week-to-week ratio showed no association and ACWR an inverse one.
sources.locator: Abstract; Methods (exposure definition); Results Table 1; Discussion, Limitations.
limitations: Observational; authors state a preventive 10% rule needs randomized evidence.
Distance, not duration; self-reported injury; binned, non-monotonic hazard ratios.
counterevidence: Weekly progression metrics were not associated with injury in the same cohort.

A non-novice whose longest current run or weekly running is below run.minimumSessionMinutes starts on the walk/jog ladder at the highest step whose jogging per session is <= the longest current run and <= current weekly running divided by the walk/jog exposures of the week; no week-1 session holds more running than the longest current run (D42).

Intake loads: a pound value converts to kilograms at the nearest 0.5 kg and keeps the reported value; any other or missing unit leaves the load unknown and asked; a reported known dose above six sets starts at six.

An eligibility flag that means yes in any form (true, 1, yes, y, sim, si or sí, trimmed, in any letter case and with or without accents) routes CLINICAL_HUMAN_REQUIRED; any other non-boolean flag leaves eligibility unassessed (ASK), never clearance and never assumed illness.

confidence.rationale: Envelope evidence is indirect but convergent; the D42 cap applies the existing week-1 rule and was verified over the full probe grid.

limitations: Onboarding facts are self-report; wearable history may be partial.
No evidence validates the exact starter doses or establishment length.
Profiles outside V1 (elite, adolescent, pregnancy/postpartum, clinical) are excluded, not evaluated.

The interruption-reason text screen is a lexicon heuristic; any further lexical residual is an owned open gap, and the structured category plus current eligibility (dated after the break, every clinical flag false) remain the primary defence.
The familiar start rests on self-reported longest and weekly running; equivalence of intermittent and continuous jogging is unstudied.

answers.answer: The cold-start envelope is adequate for eligible V1 adults when it starts at or below current exposure.
Onboarding facts carry provenance (self-report, wearable full/partial); week-1 exposure is the material fact.
KEEP in the sense of a minimal establishment program is defensible; unknown tolerance remains unknown.
Change versus HOLD is necessary: HOLD by default leaves eligible athletes without a program.
Smallest: week 1 bounded by current exposure, with walk/jog for current running under the minimum session, starting at the ladder step whose session jogging fits the longest current run.
Smaller alternatives (no program, ASK for perfect history) fail the goal and ask for facts onboarding does not collect.
The trade-off protects long-term progression by starting low and gating steps on execution.
Evidence supports starting and progressing conservatively, not the exact starter doses.
Uncertain: self-report accuracy, individual tolerance, intermittent-versus-continuous equivalence, optimal establishment length.
ASK for missing eligibility/goal/days; CLINICAL_HUMAN_REQUIRED for clinical flags or illness/injury-named pauses.

sources.population_design_dose: 43 resistance-trained adults (>=1 y), 8 wk, 4 sets of 4 lower-body exercises 2x/wk; load progression versus repetition progression.
sources.findings: Both progressions produced similar hypertrophy, strength and endurance; small differences of questionable practical significance.
limitations: Trained participants; 8 weeks; lower body only.
counterevidence: Strength slightly favoured load progression.

sources.title: Objective Accuracy in Estimating Repetitions in Reserve in the Back Squat: An Analysis between Experienced vs. Novice Subjects
sources.authors: Droguett FAB, Festa RR, Quintana NAT, Gomez-Lopez J, Ojeda AH, Farias-Valenzuela C, et al.
sources.population_design_dose: 16 adults (8 with <18 months training), Smith-machine squat at 70% 1RM, RIR3 and RIR1 sets.
sources.findings: Accuracy of RIR3 and RIR1 estimates did not differ between experienced and less experienced participants.
limitations: n=16; single exercise; less-experienced group still had training history.
counterevidence: Meta-analytic data show average underprediction near one repetition with large heterogeneity (R6-S13).

sources.title: Accuracy in Predicting Repetitions to Task Failure in Resistance Exercise: A Scoping Review and Exploratory Meta-analysis
sources.authors: Halperin I, Malleron T, Har-Nir I, Androulakis-Korakakis P, Wolf M, Fisher J, Steele J
sources.population_design_dose: 12 studies, 414 healthy participants predicting repetitions to failure.
sources.findings: Participants underpredicted repetitions to failure by about 0.95 repetitions (95% CI 0.17-1.73) with very high heterogeneity; accuracy improved closer to failure and at <=12 repetitions.
limitations: Abstract only; full text not accessed.
counterevidence: Heterogeneity prevents an individual error estimate.

sources.title: Are Trainees Lifting Heavy Enough? Self-Selected Loads in Resistance Exercise: A Scoping Review and Exploratory Meta-analysis
sources.authors: Steele J, Malleron T, Har-Nir I, Androulakis-Korakakis P, Wolf M, Fisher JP, Halperin I
sources.population_design_dose: 18 studies, 368 healthy trainees selecting their own loads with a 1RM test.
sources.findings: On average trainees selected about 53% of 1RM (95% CrI 49-58%), with little moderation by experience, sex or age; heavier loads at lower repetition targets.
limitations: Abstract only; mostly single sessions with vague instructions.
counterevidence: Load choice depends on the repetition target and instructions.

sources.title: Self-Selected Resistance Exercise Load: Implications for Research and Prescription
sources.authors: Barbosa-Netto S, d'Acelino-e-Porto OS, Almeida MB
sources.population_design_dose: 160 trained men; the load they usually lift for 10 repetitions on bench press, then repetitions to failure with it.
sources.findings: They completed 16 +/- 5 repetitions with their usual 10-repetition load; only 22% completed 10-12.
limitations: Abstract only; one exercise; trained men.
counterevidence: Self-report of usual load, not observed training.

sources.title: Repetitions in Reserve Is a Reliable Tool for Prescribing Resistance Training Load
sources.authors: Lovegrove S, Hughes LJ, Mansfield SK, Read PJ, Price P, Patterson SD
sources.population_design_dose: 15 young novice-trained men; deadlift and bench press; load ramped to 1 RIR for 3, 5 and 8 repetitions on two testing sessions after familiarization.
sources.findings: Test-retest reliability of the RIR-selected load was high (deadlift ICC 0.95-0.99, CV 2.7-5.7%; bench press ICC 0.97-0.99, CV 3.8-6.2%).
limitations: Abstract only; small sample of young men; 1 RIR, not the 2-4 RIR used here; two barbell exercises.
counterevidence: Reliability under supervision may exceed self-logged reliability.

claims.statement: Perceived-exertion or RIR-guided selection of absolute load is an accepted way to set and progress load; a wide load range produces hypertrophy and failure is unnecessary, so a conservative reserve target is compatible with adaptation.
limitations: No trial tests this exact establishment protocol.
counterevidence: Novices may under-select load; progression rules must correct it.

claims.statement: RIR estimates are approximate: average underprediction near one repetition with high heterogeneity; accuracy at RIR 1-3 did not differ by experience in a small study.
limitations: Small study; abstract-only meta-analysis.
counterevidence: Accuracy in never-trained people is not established.

claims.statement: Sex, body mass or another exercise do not provide a valid individual load.
limitations: Principle-level; no conversion evidence exists.
counterevidence: None located.

claims.statement: Given free choice, trainees select on average about 53% of 1RM and loads lighter than their repetition target implies, so a logged load above the plan is uncommon; a single establishment log cannot be checked against any individual reference because no load may be derived from sex, body size or another exercise.
limitations: Abstract-level access for the two load-selection studies; mostly single sessions with vague instructions.
counterevidence: Trainees choose heavier loads at lower repetition targets.

claims.statement: Progressive overload proceeds from the load lifted under the target and reserve condition; a heavier self-selected load that missed the target or the reserve is not evidence for a load step.
limitations: No trial tests self-selected over-plan loads as a gating input.
counterevidence: RIR estimates carry about one repetition of error.

claims.statement: How implausible logged values are detected is measurement semantics owned by Data; this record only requires that an unconfirmed single establishment log never becomes a numeric prescription.
limitations: No evidence base; Data-owned semantics.
counterevidence: None.

claims.statement: Loads selected to a fixed reps-in-reserve target were highly reproducible between sessions in young novice lifters (ICC 0.95-0.99, CV 2.7-6.2%), and reps-in-reserve estimates carry about one repetition of error; one smallest increment is at or above that session-to-session variability for most loads, so agreement within one increment is a reasonable consistency check on a logged number. It is not a plausibility check.
limitations: Abstract-level access; 15 young men at 1 RIR; two barbell exercises.
One increment is a coarse share of light dumbbell loads (2 kg on 16 kg per hand).
counterevidence: Two consistent recording errors (a repeated unit or digit slip) pass any agreement check.

claims.statement: Until a first logged load is confirmed, effort-guided selection to the reserve target is the supported way to choose the next load: reps-in-reserve estimates were similarly accurate in novice and experienced lifters at moderate reserve, and current guidance supports perceived-exertion-based loading. An instruction to reuse an unconfirmed logged number replaces that evidence with a possible recording error.
claims.applicability: Healthy adults selecting loads by effort.
limitations: Small acute samples; RIR accuracy varies by exercise and proximity to failure.
counterevidence: None located.

records.applicability: Reusable envelope for the stated adult recreational nonclinical V1 population in the offline synthetic Node24 reference; concrete generated sessions inside the envelope need no paper of their own; no real-athlete effect.

decision.rationale: D44 and D45 are resolved in mechanism. An above-plan load becomes the reference only when that week's exercise gate is ADVANCE or EARNED, which is the criterion I required; a converging-fatigue hold also blocks it, which is conservative and consistent with "no adverse response". A first establishment log is no longer a number: it becomes one when confirmed, repeated within one increment, or matched to the athlete's own hint, and it is asked about until then. One smallest increment is a sound agreement tolerance. Two agreeing logs from separate sessions in the same week are as informative as logs from separate weeks for a recording check. Two consistent implausible logs, or an athlete-confirmed implausible value, are accepted inside D45, because plausibility belongs to Data. One residual must be fixed before the freeze: the pending row still tells the athlete to "use the load you logged last time" before the effort rule (D48), which brings the unconfirmed number back through the instruction. The fix is runtime text only.
preserve: Authority split: science bounds envelopes, Coaching Intelligence selects inside them.
Clinical routing and ASK for missing eligibility.
Fail-closed behaviour when the boundary is not enabled.
modify: D48 (R6-LOAD-ESTABLISHMENT; residual of D45) r6-prescription.mjs exerciseRow instructions for a FROM_LOG row whose load is pending confirmation (r6-program.mjs strengthDose, PENDING_RULE): the row correctly carries no number, but its first instruction still reads 'Use the load you logged last time for this exercise', before the rule 'Choose the load by effort as in your first session...'. When the unconfirmed log is a recording error (160 or 26 kg per hand logged for 16), the first line points the athlete at that value, which is what D45 exists to prevent (probe N). Required: a row whose load is pending confirmation states only effort-guided selection as at establishment (ramp up in the smallest increments, stop at the reserve shown) and never tells the athlete to use the logged load; add the assertion to the D45 test. No policy change is needed.
decision.mec_change_level: No change to the reviewed envelope; required runtime changes are binding corrections.
decision.trade_off: Possible early under-dosing accepted to avoid an invented or excessive first load.
must_not: Present any value as validated physiology, an injury-prevention threshold or a guarantee.
Substitute a training dose for clinical assessment.
Treat missing data as adverse or as tolerance.
Change official plan state or completed history.
conditions: Scope: offline synthetic Node24 reference only, for the adult (18+) recreational nonclinical V1 population stated in PROGRAM_POLICY_R6.population. Missing current eligibility is ASK; pain, injury, illness, functional limitation or a clinical interruption reason is CLINICAL_HUMAN_REQUIRED with no substitute dose.

Operational values are reversible coaching choices inside the envelope, never physiological thresholds, injury-prevention rules, readiness scores, finish-time promises or individual-response predictions.
Steps advance only on executed comparable work without an adverse signal; nothing progresses from elapsed calendar time alone; completed history and official plan state stay immutable.
Athletes with strength class NONE complete unloaded or light-implement practice before any effort-guided loaded set; the first loaded exposure is at most 2 sets at RIR >= 3.

The establishment instruction describes an ascending ramp: start with the lightest available load and add the smallest increment between preparatory sets while at least the target reserve remains with stable technique; the working load is the heaviest such load; load and convention are recorded.
No kilogram is derived from sex, body mass, another exercise or implement; a stale or differently configured known load is only a hint or ceiling.

After establishment, a load or repetition step requires a logged set record meeting target repetitions with reserve >= prescribed RIR - 1; otherwise the dose holds. A logged load above the planned load is adopted only when that exposure meets this criterion and only up to one smallest increment above the plan, never above a re-establishment ceiling; otherwise the planned load stays the reference and the logged load is asked about. A logged load at or below the plan is executed evidence; a changed known load is a modification (D44).
RIR is treated as approximate (about one repetition of error); technique and comfort govern continuation and stopping.
Fail-closed: no ESTABLISH rows are emitted when this boundary is not enabled.

A load logged on an establishment row becomes a prescribed numeric (KNOWN) load only after the athlete confirms it (in kilograms or pounds, in the planned convention), after a second logged exposure of the exercise in a separate session (later, or earlier in the same week) within establishmentAgreementIncrements smallest increment of it, or when it lies within one smallest increment of the athlete's own load hint in the same convention. Until then the next exposure is FROM_LOG with no number, its instructions describe effort-guided selection only and never point to the logged value (D48), and the logged value is asked about. Numeric plausibility of a confirmed or repeated value is Data-owned (D45).

Loads are kilograms in the engine: a pound value (intake or log) converts at the nearest 0.5 kg and keeps the reported value; another or missing unit, or a logged convention different from the planned one, is never adopted and is asked about; no prescription carries pounds or a known load above 500 kg.

An above-plan logged load is adopted only when that exercise's gate for the week is ADVANCE or EARNED; a missing reps-in-reserve log, an adverse response or a converging-fatigue hold keeps the planned load and the load is asked about (D44).

confidence.rationale: Principle-level evidence; every D44 and D45 path was exercised by direct probes; tolerance evidence is abstract-level.

limitations: Evidence for RIR accuracy in never-trained adults is thin.
Self-selected loads by novices tend to be conservative; early weeks may under-dose.
Self-selected load evidence is abstract-level; plausibility rules for logged values are Data-owned.
The agreement tolerance is a data-consistency rule; plausibility of repeated or confirmed values is Data-owned and not yet defined.

answers.answer: Adequate when known current loads are absent and movement competence is the gate.
Material facts: absence of a current known dose, declared experience, equipment.
KEEP without a load is not executable; unknown remains unknown and is resolved in-session.
Establishment is necessary versus fabricated kilograms (invalid) or withholding strength (goal loss).
Smallest intervention: practice first, then at most 2 effort-guided sets.
Smaller alternatives leave the strength goal unprogrammed or invent a load.
Protects later progression by producing a logged load basis.
Evidence supports effort-guided selection with error and progression from the load actually lifted under the target, not adoption of a heavier self-selected load that missed it.
Uncertain: beginner RIR accuracy, time to reach an effective load.
ASK when a logged load is above the plan without the ADVANCE criterion, when a first establishment log is unconfirmed, or when a unit or convention is unknown; Data owns plausibility rules.

R6-POLICY-2 probes on the current runtime: walk/jog one ladder step per week under repeated easier responses; no threshold or strides after three missed weeks; no +1 set after a fully missed block; logged RIR 1 against prescribed RIR 3 holds; squat stays at 100 kg without exercise logs; restart and walk/jog transitions declared and capped; long-run share <= 0.45 in every week of profile A; no long-run drop outside planned reductions in any profile after the share amendment; profile C runtime long run 70, 70, then consolidation 65.
Judgment call accepted: unknown logged RIR holds the dose without regression (UNKNOWN_RIR_TRAIL shows a stable hold).

R6-POLICY-3 at hash e9c87e09...: run.singleRunCeiling.reference uses the reviewed entry as the ceiling in every week with no run in the window (test QRE-R6-09, over 500 generated runs); strength.setsAfterReestablishment returns one set per executed week (test QRE-R6-17); learning.missingGate holds dimensions without an executed session in reviews (test QRE-R6-04; probe K: with every run missed the walk/jog step stays at 2 for eight weeks).

Remaining: the projection still advances dimensions with no planned session (D46, probe L); logged loads above the plan are adopted without the ADVANCE criterion (D44); the familiar walk/jog start can exceed the longest current run (D42).

R6-POLICY-4 at hash 1046ad0e...: learning.missingGate amended (D46), with belowMinimumSession (D42) and loggedLoadAdoption (D44). Probe L: no dimension advances in a projected week without a planned session of it (round 7: the walk/jog ladder advanced through race and post-event weeks). Probe P: no ladder or restart step on taper, race-window or post-event weeks in 360 programs. Probe M: above-plan loads only on the ADVANCE criterion. Probe B: D42 holds.

D46 side effects, not blocking: (1) an athlete whose every easy day is a walk (EASY_LOW, 15 min/week over three chosen run days) never converts a walk back to a run, in projection or after executed reviews, because conversion is gated on an executed easy session that cannot exist; the single long run grows from 15 to 60 minutes over 16 weeks while the negotiation item promises conversion at block starts (probe T; recommendation R12). sources.title: Individualized Endurance Training Based on Recovery and Training Status in Recreational Runners
sources.authors: Nuuttila OP, Nummela A, Korhonen E, Hakkinen K, Kyrolainen H
sources.population_design_dose: 30 recreational runners, matched-pair randomized, 15 wk; predefined program (2 progressive weeks with +10% volume then a -25% recovery week) versus load adjusted twice weekly from HRV, perceived recovery and HR-speed index.
sources.findings: Both groups improved; individualized group improved 10-km time more (-6.2% versus -2.9%) with fewer low responders; HIT block used 6x3 min at maximal sustainable effort.
limitations: Small sample; HRV-dependent monitoring; negligible strength training.
counterevidence: Predefined progression was also effective.

sources.title: American College of Sports Medicine Position Stand. Resistance Training Prescription for Muscle Function, Hypertrophy, and Physical Performance in Healthy Adults: An Overview of Reviews
sources.authors: Currier BS, D'Souza AC, Singh MAF, Lowisz CV, Rawson ES, Schoenfeld BJ, Smith-Ryan AE, et al.
sources.population_design_dose: Overview of 137 systematic reviews of randomized trials in healthy adults (>=18 y), resistance training >=6 wk; most evidence from novice trainees.
sources.findings: Resistance training improves strength and hypertrophy versus control; strength enhanced by heavier loads, 2-3 sets, >=2 sessions/wk and exercise at session start; hypertrophy by >=10 sets/muscle/wk; training to failure and periodization not consistently influential; perceived-exertion scales can raise absolute load with strength gains; individualization encouraged for adherence.

limitations: Overview of reviews dominated by novice trainees; not concurrent-training or runner specific.

sources.authors: Nielsen RO, Parner ET, Nohr EA, Sorensen H, Lind M, Rasmussen S
sources.population_design_dose: 874 novice runners with GPS watches, 1 year.

counterevidence: Overall injury rates did not differ.

decision.rationale: D42, D44 and D46 are resolved. The projection now holds every dimension without a planned session, the walk/jog start fits current running, and a heavier logged load needs the ADVANCE criterion. D46 made the projection honest and exposed two conservative gaps, both recorded as recommendations: walks never convert back to runs when every easy day is a walk (R12), and a single-day return never completes in projection (R13). The block-boundary credit earned by return weeks (D49) is a binding defect in this boundary's set rules. It shows only through returns, which stay disabled at this hash, so the envelope is approved with D49 required before the freeze. Recommendation: R1 (non-blocking, coaching quality): when a strength step holds only because RIR was not logged, the next session should explicitly ask for reps in reserve on that exercise; a reviewed option is one ADVANCE after two consecutive exposures with target reps met at the planned load and no RIR, never EARNED.

Two things break the declared ceiling and the one-set-per-executed-week rule. (1) A return-entry or return-step exposure in the last week of a development block (often a consolidation week) is credited as a completed block, so the first post-return week adds a block-boundary set. (2) Step 2 is computed from the base set count, not from the dose prescribed before the break. In probe section U, 7 of 17 return timelines (moderate and long) jump from 2 to 4 back-squat sets in one week and/or exceed the sets prescribed in the last week before the break; for example s1-d35 goes 3 sets before the break, then 1, 2 and 4, and s5-d14 goes 4, then 1, 2 and 4. Exercises first set up in the return-entry week (the author-found change) follow the same path. This contradicts R6-NONCLINICAL-RETURN conditions 7 and 11 (at most moderateStepsToPrior steps to the prior executed dose; historical maxima are ceilings) and R6-PLANNED-PROGRESSION conditions 5 and 13 (block-boundary set increases count executed development weeks; after re-establishment by effort the earlier set count returns at most one set per executed week). Repeated adverse responses (two comparable within 14 days at the current dose after any regression) regress one step; a single adverse response holds.

answers.answer: A planned trajectory is adequate as a conditional proposal, not as a prediction.
Material facts are executed sessions, logged sets and responses with provenance.
KEEP (repeat the dose) is the default whenever execution or response is missing.
Progression is necessary for the stated goals but only after execution evidence.
Smallest step: one dimension, one step, referenced to completed work.
Smaller alternatives (no progression) fail goal alignment; larger (double steps) exceed reviewed limits.
Consolidation protects longer-horizon progression; MEC is kept by holding rather than regressing on single signals.
Evidence supports gated progression and rep progression; it does not support doubled steps or spikes.

sources.authors: Doma K, Nicholls A, Gahreman D, Damas F, Libardi CA, Sinclair W
sources.population_design_dose: 10 resistance-untrained heat-acclimatized men; one lower-body 6RM session; submaximal running at 24 and 48 h.
sources.findings: DOMS increased, countermovement jump reduced and the physiological cost of submaximal running increased for up to 48 h after the session.
limitations: Resistance-untrained, n=10, hot environment, single bout.
counterevidence: Repeated-bout effect reduces this impairment in accustomed lifters (R6-S10, R6-S30).

sources.title: Exercise-Induced Muscle Damage and Running Economy in Humans
sources.authors: Assumpcao CO, Lima LC, Oliveira FB, Greco CC, Denadai BS
sources.population_design_dose: Narrative review of muscle damage and running economy.
sources.findings: Unaccustomed strength or eccentric work causes muscle damage; strength exercise impaired running economy mainly at high intensity; a prior bout (repeated-bout effect) attenuates damage markers and economy changes.
limitations: Narrative review; auxiliary only.
counterevidence: Running-economy findings are equivocal across studies.

sources.title: Implications of Impaired Endurance Performance following Single Bouts of Resistance Training: An Alternate Concurrent Training Perspective
sources.authors: Doma K, Deakin GB, Bentley DJ
sources.population_design_dose: Narrative review of residual fatigue after resistance training.
sources.findings: Residual fatigue after a resistance session may impair subsequent endurance session quality for several hours to days; mechanisms include neural, kinematic, soreness and glycogen factors.
limitations: Abstract only; narrative review.
counterevidence: Link from acute impairment to chronic adaptation is not established.

sources.title: Acute Effects of Aerobic Exercise on Muscle Strength and Power in Trained Male Individuals: A Systematic Review with Meta-analysis
sources.authors: Markov A, Chaabene H, Hauser L, Behm S, Bloch W, Puta C, Granacher U
sources.population_design_dose: 15 within-group studies, trained males 18-42 y; strength or power measured <=15 min after running or cycling.
sources.findings: Aerobic exercise produced moderate acute strength declines (SMD 0.79); running produced small declines (SMD 0.28) versus cycling (0.79); >30 min larger; no effect on power proxies.
limitations: Males only; immediate effects only (<=15 min); not next-day; small subgroups.
counterevidence: Several included studies report potentiation of power after aerobic work.

sources.title: Compatibility of Concurrent Aerobic and Strength Training for Skeletal Muscle Size and Function: An Updated Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
sources.authors: Schumann M, Feuerbacher JF, Sunkeler M, Freitag N, Ronnestad BR, Doma K, Lundberg TR
sources.population_design_dose: 43 studies, healthy adults, supervised concurrent training >=4 wk versus identical strength training alone.
sources.findings: No attenuation of maximal strength (SMD -0.06) or hypertrophy (-0.01); explosive strength attenuated (-0.28), mainly when performed in the same session, not when separated by >=3 h; no moderation by running versus cycling or training status.
limitations: Heterogeneous protocols; mostly untrained or active participants; aerobic dose varies.
counterevidence: Fiber-level analysis (R6-S08) suggests a small negative effect with running.

sources.title: Order of same-day concurrent training influences some indices of power development, but not strength, lean mass, or aerobic fitness in healthy, moderately-active men after 9 weeks of training
sources.authors: Lee MJ, Ballantyne JK, Chagolla J, Hopkins WG, Fyfe JJ, Phillips SM, Bishop DJ, Bartlett JD
sources.population_design_dose: 29 moderately active men, 9 wk, 3 d/wk; cycling HIIT 3 h before or after resistance training versus resistance only.
sources.findings: Leg-press 1RM and lean mass improved similarly regardless of order; resistance-then-HIIT attenuated countermovement-jump indices.
limitations: Cycling HIIT, men, small groups; 3-h separation.
counterevidence: Order effect appeared for power when strength preceded HIIT, opposite to a simple strength-first rule.

sources.title: The Role of Intra-Session Exercise Sequence in the Interference Effect: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis
sources.authors: Eddens L, van Someren K, Howatson G
sources.population_design_dose: 10 studies, healthy adults, >=5-wk concurrent programs, both modes within <=15 min in the same session.
sources.findings: Resistance-then-endurance order favoured lower-body dynamic strength (weighted mean difference 6.91%, 95% CI 1.96-11.87); no order effect for lower-body hypertrophy, static strength, VO2max or body fat.
limitations: Ten studies; mixed endurance modalities and training status; same-session only.
counterevidence: No order effect on hypertrophy or aerobic capacity.

sources.title: Effects of concurrent training sequence on VO2max and lower limb strength performance: A systematic review and meta-analysis
sources.authors: Gao J, Yu L
sources.population_design_dose: 19 RCTs, 482 participants comparing strength-endurance with endurance-strength same-session order.
sources.findings: Strength-first improved lower-limb strength more (SMD 0.19, 95% CI 0.02-0.37); no VO2max difference.
limitations: Small pooled effect; effect concentrated in subgroups (older adults, women, >8 wk).
counterevidence: No difference in lower-limb power.

sources.title: The Effects of Concurrent Aerobic and Strength Training on Muscle Fiber Hypertrophy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
sources.authors: Lundberg TR, Feuerbacher JF, Sunkeler M, Schumann M
sources.population_design_dose: 15 studies comparing concurrent training with strength training alone on fiber cross-sectional area.
sources.findings: Small negative effect on fiber hypertrophy (SMD -0.23); type I fiber hypertrophy attenuated when aerobic training was running (SMD -0.81); no moderation by same-session order.
limitations: Small number of studies; biopsy-based outcomes.
counterevidence: Whole-muscle hypertrophy not attenuated in R6-S07.

sources.title: Specific Training Effects of Concurrent Aerobic and Strength Exercises Depend on Recovery Duration
sources.authors: Robineau J, Babault N, Piscione J, Lacome M, Bigard AX
sources.population_design_dose: 58 amateur rugby players, 7 wk, strength before aerobic with 0, 6 or 24 h recovery.
sources.findings: 0 h and to a lesser extent 6 h recovery reduced strength and aerobic gains versus 24 h.
limitations: Abstract only; rugby players; magnitude-based inference.
counterevidence: R6-S07 found no maximal-strength attenuation with >=3 h separation.

sources.title: Maintaining Physical Performance: The Minimal Dose of Exercise Needed to Preserve Endurance and Strength Over Time
sources.authors: Spiering BA, Mujika I, Sharp MA, Foulis SA
sources.population_design_dose: Narrative review of maintenance doses in general populations, athletes and military.
sources.findings: Strength and muscle size maintained up to 32 wk with one session per week and one set per exercise if relative load is maintained; endurance maintained with 2 sessions/wk or 33-66% less volume if intensity is maintained.
limitations: Abstract only; narrative review; insufficient data for athletes.
counterevidence: Older adults may need more volume to maintain size.

sources.title: Effects of Short- and Long-Term Detraining on Maximal Oxygen Uptake in Athletes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
sources.authors: Zheng J, Pan T, Jiang Y, Shen Y
sources.population_design_dose: 21 studies of trained individuals after training cessation.
sources.findings: VO2max decreased after short-term (ES -0.62) and more after long-term cessation (ES -1.42).
limitations: VO2max only; heterogeneous definitions of short/long; athletes.
counterevidence: No difference between 30-90 and >90 days in subgroup analysis.

sources.title: Effect of training cessation on muscular performance: a meta-analysis
sources.authors: Bosquet L, Berryman N, Dupuy O, Mekary S, Arvisais D, Bherer L, Mujika I
sources.population_design_dose: 103 studies of resistance-training cessation.
sources.findings: Training cessation decreases all components of muscular performance; magnitude depends on training status, age and cessation duration.
limitations: Abstract only; numeric time course not extracted.
counterevidence: Recreational athletes showed smaller losses than inactive people for some outcomes.

sources.title: American College of Sports Medicine Position Stand. Resistance Training Prescription for Muscle Function, Hypertrophy, and Physical Performance in Healthy Adults: An Overview of Reviews
sources.authors: Currier BS, D'Souza AC, Singh MAF, Lowisz CV, Rawson ES, Schoenfeld BJ, Smith-Ryan AE, et al.
sources.population_design_dose: Overview of 137 systematic reviews of randomized trials in healthy adults (>=18 y), resistance training >=6 wk; most evidence from novice trainees.
sources.findings: Resistance training improves strength and hypertrophy versus control; strength enhanced by heavier loads, 2-3 sets, >=2 sessions/wk and exercise at session start; hypertrophy by >=10 sets/muscle/wk; training to failure and periodization not consistently influential; perceived-exertion scales can raise absolute load with strength gains; individualization encouraged for adherence.
sources.locator: Abstract; Results (strength, hypertrophy); Discussion subsections Progressive overload, Specificity/Individualization, Variation.
limitations: Overview of reviews dominated by novice trainees; not concurrent-training or runner specific.
No per-session increment, establishment or return procedure is specified.
counterevidence: States progression is not always necessary for benefit, so planned progression is a choice, not a requirement.

sources.title: Resistance Exercise Minimal Dose Strategies for Increasing Muscle Strength in the General Population: an Overview
sources.authors: Nuzzo JL, Pinto MD, Kirk BJC, Nosaka K
sources.population_design_dose: Narrative overview of minimal-dose strategies in people not currently resistance training.
sources.findings: Once-weekly sessions and single-set programs (>=4 exercises, >=2 sessions/wk) improve strength versus no exercise.
sources.locator: Abstract; sections on Weekend Warrior and single-set training.
limitations: Overview, not systematic; untrained populations.
counterevidence: Gains concern strength increase in untrained people, not maintenance in hybrid athletes.

sources.title: How much running is too much? Identifying high-risk running sessions in a 5200-person cohort study
sources.authors: Schuster Brandt Frandsen J, Hulme A, Parner ET, Moller M, Lindman I, Abrahamson J, et al., Nielsen RO
sources.population_design_dose: 5205 adult runners (mean 45.8 y, 22% female), Garmin GPS data, 588,071 sessions, 18-month follow-up; exposure = single-session distance relative to the longest run in the previous 30 days.
sources.findings: Single-session spikes >10-30%, >30-100% and >100% above the 30-day longest run were associated with higher overuse-injury rates (HRR 1.64, 1.52, 2.28); week-to-week ratio showed no association and ACWR an inverse one.
sources.locator: Abstract; Methods (exposure definition); Results Table 1; Discussion, Limitations.
limitations: Observational; authors state a preventive 10% rule needs randomized evidence.
Distance, not duration; self-reported injury; binned, non-monotonic hazard ratios.
counterevidence: Weekly progression metrics were not associated with injury in the same cohort.

sources.title: Exercise-Induced Muscle Damage and Running Economy in Humans
sources.authors: Assumpcao CO, Lima LC, Oliveira FB, Greco CC, Denadai BS
sources.population_design_dose: Narrative review of muscle damage and running economy.
sources.findings: Unaccustomed strength or eccentric work causes muscle damage; strength exercise impaired running economy mainly at high intensity; a prior bout (repeated-bout effect) attenuates damage markers and economy changes.
limitations: Narrative review; auxiliary only.
counterevidence: Running-economy findings are equivocal across studies.

sources.title: Does Taking a Break Matter-Adaptations in Muscle Strength and Size Between Continuous and Periodic Resistance Training
sources.authors: Halonen EJ, Gabriel I, Kelahaara MM, Ahtiainen JP, Hulmi JJ
sources.population_design_dose: 55 healthy untrained adults (42 completed) randomized to periodic training (10 weeks training, 10 weeks break, 10 weeks retraining) or continuous training (20 weeks), twice weekly whole-body resistance training.
sources.findings: Strength and size fell during the break and were regained rapidly on retraining; both groups ended with similar adaptations.
limitations: Abstract only; untrained participants; a 10-week break; supervised training.
counterevidence: Rapid regain suggests that a conservative restoration may be slower than necessary.

decision.rationale: R6 and R7 are accepted. Yes-meaning eligibility flags now route to a human in every path, and other non-booleans stay unknown; that is stricter than the interruption flag and correct for eligibility. The round-7 residuals now route CLINICAL or ASK. The local-negation rule moves only locally negated damage statements from CLINICAL to ASK, never to a nonclinical return, and affirmed damage stays CLINICAL wherever else a negation sits. New residuals, mostly birth-related and procedure words, stay inside the owned gap (R11). The return-entry ceiling is correct. In return step 2 the runtime caps at the adopted entry load, which is stricter than the declared text and matches the step-2 instruction "no increase yet"; I accept it, to be declared with D49. The entry dose now covers every exposure of the entry week. The boundary stays REVISE for D49: the strength return can add two sets in the week after it and exceed the pre-break dose, contradicting its own ceiling. I missed this in earlier rounds; it predates R6-POLICY-4.
preserve: Authority split: science bounds envelopes, Coaching Intelligence selects inside them.
Clinical routing and ASK for missing eligibility.
Fail-closed behaviour when the boundary is not enabled.
modify: D49 (R6-NONCLINICAL-RETURN, shared with R6-PLANNED-PROGRESSION) r6-program.mjs advanceStrength (block-boundary credit, blocksDone) and strengthDose (return step 2 and the first weeks after the return), and policy operational.return: after a moderate or long nonclinical interruption the strength return is one set at RIR >= 4, then the base set count minus one at RIR 3, then the normal dose. Two things break the declared ceiling and the one-set-per-executed-week rule. (1) A return-entry or return-step exposure in the last week of a development block (often a consolidation week) is credited as a completed block, so the first post-return week adds a block-boundary set. (2) Step 2 is computed from the base set count, not from the dose prescribed before the break. In probe section U, 7 of 17 return timelines (moderate and long) jump from 2 to 4 back-squat sets in one week and/or exceed the sets prescribed in the last week before the break; for example s1-d35 goes 3 sets before the break, then 1, 2 and 4, and s5-d14 goes 4, then 1, 2 and 4. Exercises first set up in the return-entry week (the author-found change) follow the same path. This contradicts R6-NONCLINICAL-RETURN conditions 7 and 11 (at most moderateStepsToPrior steps to the prior executed dose; historical maxima are ceilings) and R6-PLANNED-PROGRESSION conditions 5 and 13 (block-boundary set increases count executed development weeks; after re-establishment by effort the earlier set count returns at most one set per executed week). The defect predates R6-POLICY-4 (the FREEZE-1 source has the same credit and step-2 formula); I did not detect it in rounds 1 to 7. Required: (a) return-entry and return-step exposures never count toward a block-boundary set increase; (b) after the return steps the set count returns to the last executed pre-break set count at most one set per executed week, consolidation and taper reductions applying on top, and goes above it only through a block completed with non-return executed exposures; (c) declare this in operational.return, together with the load cap as the runtime applies it (during the return steps the cap is the current return reference: the adopted entry load, otherwise the load before the break); (d) add the probe-U timelines s1-d35, s3-d21 and s5-d14 as regression tests.
decision.mec_change_level: Binding and policy revision required before enabling; no change to Product Truth.
decision.trade_off: Slower return to prior doses accepted in exchange for evidence-based re-entry.
must_not: Present any value as validated physiology, an injury-prevention threshold or a guarantee.
Substitute a training dose for clinical assessment.
Treat missing data as adverse or as tolerance.
Change official plan state or completed history.
conditions: Scope: offline synthetic Node24 reference only, for the adult (18+) recreational nonclinical V1 population stated in PROGRAM_POLICY_R6.population. Missing current eligibility is ASK; pain, injury, illness, functional limitation or a clinical interruption reason is CLINICAL_HUMAN_REQUIRED with no substitute dose.

Binding: this record binds canonical policy hash 1046ad0ef1291068b309e229852b782e8a8f0eee478c3f8aec59facedd80a554 (value.mjs hash). Any policy byte change invalidates it; any change to the runtime functions named in requiredRuntimeChanges needs a delta binding review before runtime freeze.

Operational values are reversible coaching choices inside the envelope, never physiological thresholds, injury-prevention rules, readiness scores, finish-time promises or individual-response predictions.
Steps advance only on executed comparable work without an adverse signal; nothing progresses from elapsed calendar time alone; completed history and official plan state stay immutable.

Interruption reasons are structured; any illness, injury, pain or clinical category, or a whole-word clinical-lexicon match in free text, routes CLINICAL_HUMAN_REQUIRED regardless of nonclinical or clinicalReason flags; an ambiguous or missing reason is ASK; the same rule applies to the intake pause and the legacy path.
Current eligibility must be assessed on or after the interruption end date.
SHORT (<= shortMaxDays): resume the last executed doses; the first quality slot runs easy; the next step waits for executed sessions.

MODERATE (<= moderateMaxDays): run entry from a current demonstration (modality RUN, easy/long/recovery-easy family, completed, conversational effort, compatible response, ordinary and next-day function, observed after the interruption began and within currentDemonstrationMaxAgeDays) or the reviewed 15-minute entry; at most moderateStepsToPrior conditional steps to the prior executed dose, each within the single-run ceiling of R6-PLANNED-PROGRESSION.

Strength return: every strength exposure of the return-entry week, including exercises first set up in it, is one effort-guided set at RIR >= strengthEntryMinimumRir with the prior load only as a ceiling; the prior KNOWN load is prescribed only after a post-interruption logged entry load supports it, otherwise FROM_LOG from the entry log; during the return steps a logged load above the current return reference is capped there and asked about; return weeks never count toward a block-boundary set increase, and after the return steps the set count returns at most one set per executed week to the last executed pre-break set count (D49).
LONG (> moderateMaxDays): restart class for running; strength re-establishes by effort; no prior-load KNOWN prescription until a post-interruption log exists.
EARNED is unavailable during RETURN/RESTART; surplus counts only observations after the return started.
No universal percentage rollback; historical maxima are ceilings, not current proof.

A nonclinical return requires a structured nonclinical reason category (legacy R5 contract: clinicalReason=false) and current eligibility assessed on or after the interruption end with every clinical flag false; free text can only add CLINICAL or ASK outcomes.

Interruption facts out of range or contradicting each other (days outside 1-3650 or not whole, unreal dates, start after end, dates after the review, days and dates disagreeing by more than one day) are asked, never resolved to the least conservative class; a clinical flag that means yes in any form routes to a human, one that is neither yes nor no is asked.
A run demonstration shorter than run.minimumSessionMinutes is not used as a demonstration.

Additions to the free-text screen (clinical terms, phrases, the damage-verb plus body-part rule) may only add CLINICAL or ASK outcomes; body parts alone stay ASK; a damage statement whose every damage verb is locally negated is ASK, never NONCLINICAL; a negation elsewhere in the clause never hides an affirmed damage statement.

A clinical eligibility flag that means yes in any form routes CLINICAL_HUMAN_REQUIRED in the intake, the review and the legacy path, as does a clinical status in any letter case; any other non-boolean flag leaves eligibility unassessed (ASK), never clearance and never assumed illness.

confidence.rationale: Return-dose evidence is indirect; R6, R7 and D49 were reproduced by direct probes.

limitations: Direct evidence on nonclinical pause-length dosing is sparse; length classes are operational.
Cause verification relies on self-report.

The interruption-reason text screen is a lexicon heuristic; any further lexical residual is an owned open gap, and the structured category plus current eligibility (dated after the break, every clinical flag false) remain the primary defence.
Pregnancy and postpartum are excluded at intake by a structured field, but a review or return has no structured re-check; free text is the only backstop there (R11).

answers.answer: The prior plan is not adequate unchanged after a moderate or long interruption.
Material facts: interruption length, structured cause, current eligibility, current demonstration.
KEEP is defensible only for short interruptions with executed-dose resumption.
Change is necessary versus resuming elapsed-time doses.
Smallest: entry from current evidence, prior doses as ceilings, two conditional steps, then the prior dose restored one set per executed week without block credit from the return weeks.

Restoring the prior set count at once after step 2, or crediting return weeks as a completed block, exceeds the prior executed dose without evidence; holding at the entry dose would ignore executed return sessions.
Protects goal trajectory by bounded steps without catch-up.
Evidence supports conservative re-entry, not exact step counts.
Uncertain: capacity retained, cause accuracy.
CLINICAL_HUMAN_REQUIRED for illness/injury/pain causes; ASK for unknown cause.

sources.title: Effects of tapering on performance in endurance athletes: A systematic review and meta-analysis
sources.authors: Wang Z, Wang YT, Gao W, Zhong Y
sources.population_design_dose: 14 studies in well-trained endurance athletes (VO2max >55 ml/kg/min).
sources.findings: Taper improved time-trial (SMD -0.45) and time-to-exhaustion performance; volume reductions of 41-60% with maintained intensity and frequency, durations <=7, 8-14 or 15-21 days and progressive or step tapers were effective.
limitations: Trained, not recreational, athletes; few studies per subgroup.
counterevidence: No change in VO2max or economy; benefits depend on prior overload.

sources.title: Longer Disciplined Tapers Improve Marathon Performance for Recreational Runners
sources.authors: Smyth B, Lawlor A
sources.population_design_dose: Training logs of >158,000 recreational marathon runners; taper type by weekly distance pattern.
sources.findings: Strict (progressively decreasing) and longer tapers up to 3 weeks were associated with better finish times (median 2.6% versus minimal taper).
limitations: Marathon, not 10K/HM; retrospective association; distance only.
counterevidence: Association cannot separate taper from runner selection effects.

sources.title: Maintaining Physical Performance: The Minimal Dose of Exercise Needed to Preserve Endurance and Strength Over Time
sources.authors: Spiering BA, Mujika I, Sharp MA, Foulis SA
sources.population_design_dose: Narrative review of maintenance doses in general populations, athletes and military.
sources.findings: Strength and muscle size maintained up to 32 wk with one session per week and one set per exercise if relative load is maintained; endurance maintained with 2 sessions/wk or 33-66% less volume if intensity is maintained.
limitations: Abstract only; narrative review; insufficient data for athletes.
counterevidence: Older adults may need more volume to maintain size.

sources.title: Resistance Exercise Minimal Dose Strategies for Increasing Muscle Strength in the General Population: an Overview
sources.authors: Nuzzo JL, Pinto MD, Kirk BJC, Nosaka K
sources.population_design_dose: Narrative overview of minimal-dose strategies in people not currently resistance training.
sources.findings: Once-weekly sessions and single-set programs (>=4 exercises, >=2 sessions/wk) improve strength versus no exercise.
sources.locator: Abstract; sections on Weekend Warrior and single-set training.
limitations: Overview, not systematic; untrained populations.
counterevidence: Gains concern strength increase in untrained people, not maintenance in hybrid athletes.

sources.title: The Effect of a Resistance Training Session on Physiological and Thermoregulatory Measures of Sub-maximal Running Performance in the Heat in Heat-Acclimatized Men
sources.authors: Doma K, Nicholls A, Gahreman D, Damas F, Libardi CA, Sinclair W
sources.population_design_dose: 10 resistance-untrained heat-acclimatized men; one lower-body 6RM session; submaximal running at 24 and 48 h.
sources.findings: DOMS increased, countermovement jump reduced and the physiological cost of submaximal running increased for up to 48 h after the session.
limitations: Resistance-untrained, n=10, hot environment, single bout.
counterevidence: Repeated-bout effect reduces this impairment in accustomed lifters (R6-S10, R6-S30).

sources.title: Implications of Impaired Endurance Performance following Single Bouts of Resistance Training: An Alternate Concurrent Training Perspective
sources.authors: Doma K, Deakin GB, Bentley DJ
sources.population_design_dose: Narrative review of residual fatigue after resistance training.
sources.findings: Residual fatigue after a resistance session may impair subsequent endurance session quality for several hours to days; mechanisms include neural, kinematic, soreness and glycogen factors.
limitations: Abstract only; narrative review.
counterevidence: Link from acute impairment to chronic adaptation is not established.

sources.title: Biomechanical Changes and the Time Course of Recovery in Lower Extremities of Recreational Runners Following a Simulated Treadmill Half-Marathon
sources.authors: Wang W, Xu S, Komnik I, Viellehner J, Zedler M, Potthast W
sources.population_design_dose: Recreational runners, simulated treadmill half-marathon; measures before, after, day 1 and day 2.
sources.findings: Knee torques, joint position sense and landing mechanics changed immediately after; most parameters recovered within one day and hip position sense within two days.
limitations: Treadmill simulation rather than a race; small sample.
counterevidence: Race-pace efforts may cause larger and longer disturbances.

sources.title: How much running is too much? Identifying high-risk running sessions in a 5200-person cohort study
sources.authors: Schuster Brandt Frandsen J, Hulme A, Parner ET, Moller M, Lindman I, Abrahamson J, et al., Nielsen RO
sources.population_design_dose: 5205 adult runners (mean 45.8 y, 22% female), Garmin GPS data, 588,071 sessions, 18-month follow-up; exposure = single-session distance relative to the longest run in the previous 30 days.
sources.findings: Single-session spikes >10-30%, >30-100% and >100% above the 30-day longest run were associated with higher overuse-injury rates (HRR 1.64, 1.52, 2.28); week-to-week ratio showed no association and ACWR an inverse one.
sources.locator: Abstract; Methods (exposure definition); Results Table 1; Discussion, Limitations.
limitations: Observational; authors state a preventive 10% rule needs randomized evidence.
Distance, not duration; self-reported injury; binned, non-monotonic hazard ratios.
counterevidence: Weekly progression metrics were not associated with injury in the same cohort.

sources.title: Does a run/walk strategy decrease cardiac stress during a marathon in non-elite runners?
sources.authors: Hottenrott K, Ludyga S, Schulze S, Gronwald T, Jager FS
sources.population_design_dose: 42 non-elite runners (22 men, 20 women) randomized to a run/walk strategy or running only for a marathon; treadmill tests 7 days before and 4 days after.
sources.findings: Similar finish times (04:14:25 versus 04:07:40, p=0.377); cardiac biomarkers rose similarly in both groups; run/walk allowed similar times with less muscle discomfort.
sources.locator: Abstract only (Europe PMC core record; ssctr-evidence/abstracts-r7.json).
limitations: Abstract only; marathon, not 10K or half marathon; trained finishers, not walk/jog novices.
counterevidence: Run/walk did not reduce cardiovascular load.

sources.title: Effects of tapering on performance: a meta-analysis
sources.authors: Bosquet L, Montpetit J, Arvisais D, Mujika I
sources.population_design_dose: 27 studies of competitive athletes with defined tapers and competition or field performance.
sources.findings: A taper of about 2 weeks with training volume reduced exponentially by 41-60%, intensity and frequency maintained, was the most efficient strategy.
limitations: Abstract only; competitive athletes; durations binned in days and weeks.
counterevidence: Optimal duration varies with prior load and individual.

sources.title: Scientific bases for precompetition tapering strategies
sources.authors: Mujika I, Padilla S
sources.population_design_dose: Narrative review of tapering in athletes.
sources.findings: The taper is a progressive nonlinear reduction of training load during a variable period before competition (4 to more than 28 days); keep intensity, reduce volume, reduce frequency by no more than 20%; progressive tapers outperform step tapers.
limitations: Abstract only; narrative review; athletes.
counterevidence: Durations are a wide range, not a rule.

sources.title: What are the Differences in Injury Proportions Between Different Populations of Runners? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
sources.authors: Kluitenberg B, van Middelkoop M, Diercks R, van der Worp H
sources.population_design_dose: 86 studies of injury proportions in defined runner populations (novice, recreational, track, road, marathon, ultra-marathon, cross-country), pooled by population, injury definition and follow-up period.
sources.findings: Over short follow-up, time-loss injury proportions were similar in novice (26.4%) and recreational (28.0%) runners and higher in runners training for a marathon (64.7%); one 18-month prospective novice cohort reported 84.9%; the authors suggest injury risk is greater for runners training for longer distances.
sources.locator: Abstract; Results, time-loss injuries during short and long follow-up; Discussion (ssctr-evidence/PMC4513221.xml).
limitations: Proportions, not rates per hour of exposure; high heterogeneity; definitions and follow-up periods differ.
counterevidence: Novice and recreational proportions were identical in the sensitivity analysis.

sources.title: Incidence and risk factors of running-related injuries during preparation for a 4-mile recreational running event
sources.authors: Buist I, Bredeweg SW, Bessem B, van Mechelen W, Lemmink KA, Diercks RL
sources.population_design_dose: 629 novice and recreational runners followed over an 8-week training period before a 4-mile event.
sources.findings: 25.9% reported at least one running-related injury (30.1 per 1000 h); no previous running experience was the most important risk factor in men (HR 2.6) and women (HR 2.1).
limitations: Abstract only; 4-mile event; injury defined as at least one day of restricted running.
counterevidence: Risk factors differed by sex.

literature_snapshot.counterevidence_search: Directed counterevidence searches for each claim (single-session spikes, graded-program RCT, fiber-level interference, order effects at hours of separation, excessive exercise variation, trained-versus-recreational taper populations). Search snippets were discovery only; findings are taken from full text or, where labelled, abstracts.

claims.statement: A progressive taper reducing volume by about 41-60% while maintaining intensity and frequency, over <=7 to 21 days, improves endurance time-trial performance in trained athletes.
claims.applicability: Trained endurance athletes; indirect for recreational 10K/HM.
limitations: Population indirect; few studies per subgroup.
counterevidence: Benefit depends on prior overload.

claims.statement: Recreational runners using disciplined progressive tapers had better marathon times.
limitations: Observational; marathon.
counterevidence: Selection effects.

claims.statement: Strength can be maintained over weeks with one session and one set per exercise if relative load is maintained; very low doses still stimulate strength in untrained people.
limitations: Abstract-only and narrative sources.
counterevidence: Athlete-specific data insufficient.

claims.statement: A heavy lower-body session can impair running for up to about 48 h, so stopping strength >= 3 days before the race is conservative.
limitations: Acute, untrained lifters.
counterevidence: One set at RIR >= 4 of familiar exercises is likely far less damaging.

claims.statement: After a simulated half-marathon most neuromuscular and biomechanical changes in recreational runners resolved within 1-2 days, consistent with a short no-run floor followed by optional easy running with a function check.
limitations: Treadmill simulation; small sample.
counterevidence: Race efforts may cause longer disturbance.

claims.statement: The exact taper and race-week fractions for recreational 10K/HM hybrid athletes are not validated; they are operational choices inside the progressive-taper envelope.
limitations: No direct trial.
counterevidence: None located.

claims.statement: Taper evidence defines tapers by days before competition (about 2 weeks optimal with volume reduced 41-60% in competitive athletes; tapers of 7 days or less, 8-14 and 15-21 days effective in endurance athletes; progressive nonlinear tapers preferred), so counting proximity in days to the race, a 6-day race window plus 7 taper days per taper week, is a faithful reading of the progressive-taper envelope; the 6/7-day split is operational.
claims.applicability: Trained endurance athletes; indirect for recreational 10K and half-marathon hybrid athletes.
limitations: Population indirect; abstract-only access for the 2007 meta-analysis and 2003 review.
counterevidence: Optimal duration varies with prior overload and the individual.

claims.statement: For an athlete whose preparation is walk/jog or restart running, a continuous race-effort 10K or half marathon is far longer than any prepared session; single runs far above the 30-day longest run carried the highest overuse-injury rates, and a run/walk strategy gave similar marathon times with less muscle discomfort in non-elite runners, so completion with walk breaks at conversational effort is the more conservative race-day default.
claims.applicability: Recreational athletes racing beyond their prepared running.
limitations: Observational spike data; run/walk trial in trained marathoners, abstract only.
counterevidence: The race is the athlete's own choice; no prescription makes an under-prepared race safe.

claims.statement: A continuous run that a walk/jog athlete has not yet reached is a new stimulus, not a taper reduction; the taper reduces the achieved session of the current mode.
claims.applicability: Walk/jog and restart athletes near an event.
limitations: Inference from taper and single-session evidence; no direct trial.
counterevidence: None located.

claims.statement: For an athlete whose continuous running was built inside this program from walk/jog or a restart, a 10K is a single session several times longer than any prepared run (a longest continuous run of 15-25 minutes for walk/jog-class racers in the probes). Single runs far above the 30-day longest run carried the highest overuse-injury rate in a large cohort, and having no previous running experience was the strongest injury risk factor while preparing for a recreational event. The completion default with walk breaks should therefore follow where the running came from, not only the label of the race week.
claims.applicability: Recreational athletes racing a 10K or half marathon after walk/jog or restart preparation inside the program.
limitations: Observational, distance-based spike data; the event cohort trained for a 4-mile race over 8 weeks (abstract only); no trial tests completion pacing for such athletes.
counterevidence: Over short follow-up, novice and recreational runners had similar time-loss injury proportions (R6-S40); the race is the athlete's choice and no pacing instruction makes an under-prepared race safe.

claims.statement: A meta-analysis of injury proportions found no large difference between novice (26.4%) and recreational (28.0%) runners over short follow-up, and higher proportions in runners training for longer distances; novice status alone is not the risk, the size of the race relative to prepared running is.
limitations: Proportions, not rates per hour; heterogeneous definitions.
counterevidence: One 18-month prospective novice cohort reported 84.9% time-loss injuries.

records.applicability: Reusable envelope for the stated adult recreational nonclinical V1 population in the offline synthetic Node24 reference; concrete generated sessions inside the envelope need no paper of their own; no real-athlete effect.

decision.rationale: D43(a), (c) and (e) are resolved, and R9 (for the half marathon) and R10 are adopted. Across 360 mode-varied programs no event-week session exceeds what the athlete has reached in the current mode, no step happens in event weeks, strides near the race require executed strides, and race day is a completion wherever the race-week mode is walk/jog, restart or return. D43(b) and (d) are only partly resolved. My round-7 change required the completion race day whenever EVENT_AMBITIOUS_FOR_CURRENT_RUNNING applied, and R6-POLICY-3 emitted that item for every walk/jog- or restart-class athlete. R6-POLICY-4 ties both to the race-week mode. An athlete who leaves the walk/jog ladder or the restart a few weeks before a 10K, with a longest continuous run of 15-30 minutes, now races at hard effort with an instruction to press and gets no negotiation at all, which is less disclosure than before. D47 restores the trigger by program history, keeps the half-marathon threshold, and leaves any exemption to a declared and reviewed value.

modify: D47 (R6-EVENT-TRANSITION; residual of D43(b) and (d)) r6-program.mjs raceDayCompletion and the EVENT_AMBITIOUS_FOR_CURRENT_RUNNING negotiation in generateProgram, and policy operational.event.raceDayCompletion: R6-POLICY-3 emitted EVENT_AMBITIOUS_FOR_CURRENT_RUNNING for every athlete whose run class was WALK_JOG or RESTART (FREEZE-1 source, generateProgram), and my D43(b) required a completion race day whenever that item applied. R6-POLICY-4 ties both the completion race day and the item to the run mode in race week (or a half-marathon long run below 75 minutes). An athlete who entered the program as WALK_JOG or RESTART and switched to continuous running before race week now races a 10K at 'hard but controlled' effort with 'decide in the final part whether to press', and receives no negotiation item. Probe P: 51 of 360 programs (24 walk/jog-class 10K racers whose longest planned continuous run before the race is 15-25 minutes; 27 restart-class 10K racers at 25-55 minutes). Probe C: the novice 10K in 12 weeks (longest continuous run 20 minutes; taper and race-week runs 15 minutes), the below-minimum 10K in 12 weeks and the restart 10K in 6 weeks. The negotiation detail can also read 'a longest run of 0 minutes' for an athlete who reached 25-minute easy runs without a long-run day (probe C, half marathon). Required: (a) race day is a completion prescription, and the item is emitted with both options, also when the athlete was in WALK_JOG or RESTART mode in any week of this program before the race (this covers the starting class and a restart applied by a review); (b) the item states the longest continuous run the plan reaches by race week (the larger of the achieved long and easy runs, or the continuous ladder step), never 0 when runs were reached; (c) declare both in operational.event.raceDayCompletion; any event-specific exemption for athletes who rebuild a substantial long run, like the half-marathon threshold, must be declared and reviewed, and none applies by default; (d) add the probe-C cases as regression tests.

decision.trade_off: Some strength stimulus is reduced near the race to protect race freshness.

Substitute a training dose for clinical assessment.

conditions: Scope: offline synthetic Node24 reference only, for the adult (18+) recreational nonclinical V1 population stated in PROGRAM_POLICY_R6.population. Missing current eligibility is ASK; pain, injury, illness, functional limitation or a clinical interruption reason is CLINICAL_HUMAN_REQUIRED with no substitute dose.

Binding: this record binds canonical policy hash 1046ad0ef1291068b309e229852b782e8a8f0eee478c3f8aec59facedd80a554 (value.mjs hash). Any policy byte change invalidates it; any change to the runtime functions named in requiredRuntimeChanges needs a delta binding review before runtime freeze.

Operational values are reversible coaching choices inside the envelope, never physiological thresholds, injury-prevention rules, readiness scores, finish-time promises or individual-response predictions.
Steps advance only on executed comparable work without an adverse signal; nothing progresses from elapsed calendar time alone; completed history and official plan state stay immutable.

Supported events are 10K and half-marathon only; one taper week plus the race week, progressive: taper-week easy runs within taperWeekRunVolumeRange and the long run within taperWeekLongRunRange of the executed peak; taper quality total work minutes within taperQualityWorkRange; race-week easy runs within raceWeekRunVolumeRange; the policy states these are per-session fractions.

Frequency is maintained; intensity is maintained only through work already executed in build/specific weeks; a race-effort touch at the policy dose >= raceWeekTouchMinDaysBeforeRace days before the race requires R6-RUN-QUALITY and an executed comparable quality session; shakeout strides require executed strides; otherwise easy.

Strength stays at a reduced dose: taper sets about taperStrengthSetFraction of the preceding dose at RIR >= 3; race week one session of raceWeekStrengthSets at RIR >= raceWeekStrengthMinimumRir no later than raceWeekStrengthMinDaysBeforeRace days before the race; no new exercise, load increase or rotation.

Post-event: no running before postEventFirstRunMinDaysAfterRace days; runs optional and easy within postEventEasyMinutes; one light strength session; redevelopment (NEXT_BLOCK) requires an eligibility and function assessment dated after the race; redevelopment fractions are declared in the policy.
The legacy path uses the athlete's event kind and only policy-declared fractions.
No finish-time, readiness or peak-performance claim.

Event proximity counts days to the race (raceWindowDays 6; 7 taper days per taper week before the window): race-window sessions have no long run and no quality, an optional shakeout the day before, at most one race-effort touch on the run day closest to the race that is >= raceWeekTouchMinDaysBeforeRace days out, and short easy runs; taper-day sessions take taper doses whichever calendar week they fall in; post-race sessions follow the post-event rules by days since the race; a race date marked unavailable is asked about.
In WALK_JOG or RESTART mode, taper-day, race-window and post-event run sessions are reductions or holds of the achieved session of that mode, never a continuous run the mode has not reached (D43a).

Race day is a completion prescription at conversational effort with walk breaks (jog bouts no longer than achieved), without strides and without an instruction to press, when the race-week mode is WALK_JOG, RESTART or RETURN, when the athlete was in WALK_JOG or RESTART mode in any week of the program before the race (D47), or for a half marathon whose achieved long run is below raceDayCompletion.halfMarathonAchievedLongRunBelowMinutes; race-day warm-up strides and shakeout strides for any athlete only after executed strides (D43b-c, R9).

Whenever race day is a completion, the event negotiation states the longest continuous run the plan reaches by race week (never 0 when runs were reached) and offers keep-with-walk-breaks or a later or shorter event; it may stay non-blocking for the preparatory weeks (D43d, D47).
In taper weeks and at the start of the next block the long run is never shorter than that week's easy run (R10).
Walk/jog and restart steps do not advance on taper, race-window or post-event days; the next block resumes the walk/jog ladder one step back.

confidence.rationale: The day-based taper reading is well grounded; D47 was reproduced by direct probes; recreational applicability stays indirect.

limitations: Taper evidence is from trained athletes; recreational evidence observational.
Combined run+strength taper evidence is indirect.
Post-event recovery evidence is from a simulated half-marathon.
The 6-day race window and the 7-day taper-day split are operational; completion with walk breaks is supported only indirectly (run/walk trial in marathoners, abstract only).
Which rebuilt long run, if any, should exempt a walk/jog- or restart-class athlete from the completion default is not established; no exemption applies until one is declared and reviewed.

answers.answer: The build plan is not adequate unchanged near the event; a taper is required.
Material facts: event date and kind, executed peak sessions, post-race eligibility.
KEEP build doses into race week is not defensible.
Reduction is necessary; the comparator is ordinary continuation.

Smallest: day-based taper with frequency kept and no new stimulus; for athletes whose running was built from walk/jog or a restart in this program, event sessions that follow the mode and a completion race day with walk breaks.
A trigger based only on the race-week mode is not enough: athletes who switched to continuous running weeks before the race still have far less continuous running than the race demands.
Strength kept at low dose protects the strength goal without race interference.
Evidence supports progressive volume reduction with maintained intensity, not exact fractions.
Uncertain: recreational response, combined taper interaction.

CLINICAL_HUMAN_REQUIRED for post-race pain or illness; ASK when post-race eligibility or the race date is missing; the keep-or-change event decision for under-prepared athletes is asked without blocking the preparatory weeks.

sources.authors: Saw AE, Main LC, Gastin PB
